facts.title: Image scanners see packages, not reachable code paths
facts.fact: Most image scanners inventory OS packages and language dependencies, then match them against vulnerability databases. They cannot see whether a vulnerable function is reachable, whether a bundled binary was compiled from the package they identified, or whether a distroless image has no package database at all. Scan results therefore need triage: package origin, fixed version availability, exposure of the component at runtime, and whether the image is actually deployed.
details: Scratch and distroless images may yield no OS packages, so scanners that rely solely on `/var/lib/dpkg` or `rpm` report nothing.
Go and Rust binaries often embed dependency versions; scanner support for those ecosystems varies by tool and build flags.
Continuous registry scanning matters because a clean scan at build time says nothing about CVEs published next week.
pitfalls: Treating a scanner's critical count as the number of exploitable issues.
Scanning only at build and never re-scanning images already running in production.

commands.purpose: Scan a pinned image for high and critical issues that have fixes available.
Cross-check findings with a second scanner to reduce tool-specific blind spots.

mcqs.question: Why can an image scanner report zero findings for a distroless image that still contains a vulnerable Go binary?
options: Distroless images cannot contain vulnerabilities
The image has no OS package database for the scanner to enumerate, and binary dependency metadata may not be detected
Go binaries are exempt from CVE matching
Scanners only scan running containers
mcqs.rationale: Package-database scanners need package metadata. Distroless images lack it, and embedded Go module information is not always parsed, so absence of findings is not evidence of safety.

misconceptions.claim: A clean image scan means the workload has no known vulnerabilities.
misconceptions.correction: Scans cover what the tool can enumerate, usually OS packages and lockfile dependencies. They miss reachability, vendored or statically linked code, and CVEs published after the scan.

references.title: NIST SP 800-190: Application Container Security Guide

facts.title: Verify a signature against an identity, not just the fact of a signature
facts.fact: Sigstore cosign can sign an image with a key pair or keylessly: the signer authenticates with an OIDC identity, Fulcio issues a short-lived certificate binding that identity to a key, and the signature is recorded in the Rekor transparency log. Verification must therefore check the expected certificate identity and issuer; accepting any valid signature lets anyone who can sign an image pass the check. Admission policies should enforce the verification rule at deploy time.
details: A keyless verification command uses `--certificate-identity` and `--certificate-oidc-issuer`; both are required for a meaningful check.
`cosign verify-attestation` verifies a signed in-toto attestation, such as an SBOM or SLSA provenance predicate.
Key-pair signing is still supported and is useful where OIDC is unavailable, but the public key becomes a distribution problem.
pitfalls: Running `cosign verify` without identity constraints and treating a successful signature check as proof of trusted authorship.
Signing only the tag at release time while deploying by a digest that was never signed.

commands.purpose: Verify that the image was signed by a specific workflow at a specific tag.
Keyless-sign a digest using the caller's OIDC identity.

mcqs.question: What must a verifier supply to make a keyless cosign verification meaningful?
options: Only the image digest
The expected certificate identity and OIDC issuer
The registry password
The Rekor private key
mcqs.rationale: Keyless signatures are valid for whoever obtained the certificate. Pinning the expected identity and issuer is what binds the signature to a trusted build workflow.

facts.title: Docker Content Trust signs tags in the Docker CLI, not at the cluster
facts.fact: Docker Content Trust uses Notary (TUF-based) metadata to sign tag-to-digest mappings when `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1` is set. It protects against a compromised registry serving a different image for a tag, but enforcement happens in the Docker client: Kubernetes, containerd and most managed runtimes do not verify DCT metadata by default. A cluster therefore needs an admission policy based on cosign or an equivalent verifier to enforce image trust.
details: DCT distinguishes the snapshot, targets, timestamp and root keys, and supports delegation roles for multiple signers.
Signing a tag does not automatically sign every future digest pushed under that tag; each push must be signed.
Notary v1 is legacy; Sigstore cosign is the common choice for Kubernetes admission verification.
pitfalls: Enabling DCT in a developer's shell and concluding that the cluster only runs signed images.
Losing the root key and being unable to rotate or add delegations for the repository.

commands.purpose: Push and sign the tag with Docker Content Trust enabled in the client.
Show the signers and keys associated with a trusted tag.

mcqs.question: A team enables Docker Content Trust for pushes. Does a Kubernetes cluster reject an unsigned image pulled from the same registry?
options: Yes, because the registry enforces signatures
No, DCT enforcement is client-side; the cluster needs its own verification policy
Yes, containerd verifies DCT metadata by default
Only if the image is pinned by digest
mcqs.rationale: DCT protects the Docker client's pull and push operations. Kubernetes and containerd do not enforce Notary metadata by default, so admission control is required for cluster-side enforcement.

misconceptions.claim: Signing an image in the registry means every runtime will refuse to run it if it is tampered with.
misconceptions.correction: A signature is only effective where it is verified. Most orchestrators do not verify signatures by default; you need an admission controller or policy engine that checks the signature and identity before admitting the workload.

references.title: Docker Docs: Content trust in Docker
NIST SP 800-190: Application Container Security Guide

facts.title: An SBOM is an inventory; it does not assert that anything is safe
facts.fact: A software bill of materials lists the components and versions in an image, usually as SPDX or CycloneDX JSON. Generating one with a tool such as Syft gives downstream consumers a way to answer 'is this component present' without pulling and unpacking the image. An SBOM is not a vulnerability report and does not include exploitability; it becomes useful when paired with a vulnerability database, VEX statements and an inventory of where the image runs.
details: SPDX and CycloneDX differ in structure but both can express packages, versions and relationships; pick one and record the format version.
Syft can scan an image, a directory or an archive and can also emit the SBOM as a signed attestation with cosign.
NTIA's minimum elements for an SBOM include supplier, component name, version, dependency relationships and a unique identifier.
pitfalls: Treating the presence of an SBOM as proof that the image was scanned or patched.
Storing SBOMs but never joining them to deployment data, so you cannot answer which running workloads contain a newly disclosed component.

commands.purpose: Generate an SPDX JSON SBOM for a container image.
Generate the same inventory in CycloneDX format for a consumer that requires it.

mcqs.question: What can an SBOM directly tell you?
options: Which components and versions are present in the artifact
Which components are reachable at runtime
Whether the artifact contains exploitable vulnerabilities
Whether the build was reproducible
mcqs.rationale: An SBOM is a component inventory. Reachability, exploitability and build reproducibility require additional evidence such as call-graph analysis, VEX and provenance.

facts.title: Base image choice drives most of the OS-level CVE count
facts.fact: The base image determines which OS packages, shell utilities and TLS libraries ship in every derived image, so a large general-purpose base produces far more vulnerability findings than a minimal or distroless base. Triage should first ask whether the base is still supported, whether a newer digest fixes the finding, and whether the affected package is reachable in the running process. Rebuilding on a regular cadence is required because a pinned digest does not receive fixes automatically.
details: An end-of-life distribution base will not receive security updates even if the image is rebuilt.
`docker scout cves` and `docker scout recommendations` can suggest a newer base or a smaller alternative.
Some findings are in packages that are never invoked, such as a shell in an image whose entrypoint runs a static binary; removing the package is better than suppressing the finding.
pitfalls: Chasing a lower CVE count by switching to `scratch` without providing CA certificates and timezone data.
Suppressing findings globally instead of fixing the base image or documenting a time-bound exception.

commands.purpose: List fixable high and critical CVEs in an image.
Inspect image labels for base-image and build metadata used in triage.

references.title: NIST SP 800-190: Application Container Security Guide

facts.title: Role and RoleBinding grant namespace-scoped access; ClusterRole does not have to
facts.fact: Kubernetes RBAC grants permissions through a rule holder (Role or ClusterRole) and a binding (RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding). A Role lives in one namespace and a RoleBinding grants its rules only there, while a ClusterRoleBinding grants cluster-wide. A RoleBinding may also reference a ClusterRole, which is how a shared set of rules is granted in a single namespace without duplicating the rules.
details: Rules specify apiGroups, resources and verbs; `resources: ["pods/log"]` is a subresource grant distinct from `pods`.
`kubectl auth can-i` with `--as` impersonation is the quickest way to test an intended grant without changing credentials.
The `bind` and `escalate` verbs allow a subject to create bindings or roles that exceed its own permissions and should be tightly restricted.
pitfalls: Using a ClusterRoleBinding for a namespace-scoped need, granting access in every namespace.
Granting `create` on pods without considering that a pod can mount any service account token or host path the admission policy allows.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: team-alpha
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
configs.purpose: Read-only Role for pods and pod logs in one namespace.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: pod-reader-binding
  namespace: team-alpha
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: report-reader
    namespace: team-alpha
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
configs.purpose: Bind the pod-reader Role to one service account in the same namespace.

commands.code: kubectl auth can-i list pods --namespace team-alpha --as=system:serviceaccount:team-alpha:report-reader
commands.purpose: Test whether a service account can list pods in a namespace.

mcqs.question: A RoleBinding in namespace team-alpha references a ClusterRole named viewer. What access does it grant?
options: The ClusterRole's rules in every namespace
The ClusterRole's rules only in team-alpha
Nothing, because RoleBindings cannot reference ClusterRoles
Only access to the ClusterRole object itself
mcqs.rationale: A RoleBinding always grants within its own namespace, even when the referenced ClusterRole is cluster-scoped. Cluster-wide grants require a ClusterRoleBinding.

facts.title: Disable service account token automount where the workload does not call the API
facts.fact: Kubernetes mounts a projected service account token into pods by default, and since the bound service account token feature became the norm, that token is time-limited and audience-bound rather than a permanent Secret. Any process in the pod can read the token and use the pod's RBAC, so workloads that never call the Kubernetes API should set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the ServiceAccount or the pod. The token is still a credential: audit what its role can do and prefer dedicated, minimal roles.
details: Set the field on the ServiceAccount to cover every pod that uses it, and on the pod spec when a single workload needs an exception.
Projected tokens default to roughly one hour and are rotated by the kubelet; `expirationSeconds` can shorten or lengthen that within API server limits.
A pod that can create pods in its namespace can often escalate by launching a pod with a more privileged service account.
pitfalls: Leaving automount enabled on a workload that only talks to a database, giving an attacker a cluster credential for free.
Assuming the token is harmless because it is short-lived; it is valid for its whole lifetime and can be exfiltrated.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: report-reader
  namespace: team-alpha
automountServiceAccountToken: false
configs.purpose: Prevent automatic token projection for every pod using this service account.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: batch-job
  namespace: team-alpha
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
    - name: job
      image: registry.example.com/team-alpha/job@sha256:252f10c83610ebca1a059c0bae8255eba2f95be4d1d7bcfa89d7248a82d9f111
configs.purpose: Pod-level override that keeps the API token out of a job that does not need it.

mcqs.question: Which setting removes the Kubernetes API credential from a pod that does not need it?
options: securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true
automountServiceAccountToken: false
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
enableServiceLinks: false
mcqs.rationale: automountServiceAccountToken controls whether the projected token is mounted. The other settings harden the process or environment but do not remove the API credential.

references.title: Kubernetes Documentation: Configure Service Accounts for Pods

facts.title: A pod with no NetworkPolicy selecting it accepts all traffic
facts.fact: NetworkPolicy is additive and default-allow: traffic is permitted unless at least one policy selects the pod and isolates the direction. A common baseline is a policy with an empty podSelector and an Ingress policyType, which selects every pod in the namespace and denies all ingress not explicitly allowed by another policy. Enforcement depends on the CNI plugin; the API server accepts policies even when the network plugin ignores them.
details: An empty `podSelector: {}` matches every pod in the namespace; the policy has no effect outside that namespace.
Isolation is per direction: adding an Ingress policy does not restrict egress.
DNS egress must be allowed explicitly once egress is isolated, usually to kube-system on port 53.
pitfalls: Applying a default-deny policy on a CNI that does not implement NetworkPolicy and believing traffic is blocked.
Forgetting that hostNetwork pods and traffic to node-local services can bypass some policy implementations.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: team-alpha
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
configs.purpose: Deny all ingress to every pod in the namespace unless another policy allows it.

commands.code:
kubectl get networkpolicy -n team-alpha -o wide
kubectl describe networkpolicy default-deny-ingress -n team-alpha
commands.purpose: Review which pods a namespace policy selects and which policy types it declares.

mcqs.question: A namespace contains pods but no NetworkPolicy objects. What is the default traffic behaviour?
options: All pod-to-pod traffic is denied until a policy is created
All pod-to-pod traffic is allowed because there is no isolation
Only traffic from the same namespace is allowed
Traffic depends on the RBAC role of each pod
mcqs.rationale: NetworkPolicy is default-allow. A pod is isolated only when a policy selects it and lists the direction in policyTypes, so an empty namespace permits all traffic.

misconceptions.claim: Creating any NetworkPolicy in a namespace blocks all traffic by default.
misconceptions.correction: Isolation applies only to pods selected by a policy and only for the directions listed in policyTypes. Pods not selected by any policy remain fully reachable.

facts.title: NetworkPolicy peers combine with AND inside an element and OR across elements
facts.fact: In a NetworkPolicy ingress or egress rule, a single peer element that contains both a namespaceSelector and a podSelector matches pods that satisfy both conditions. Separate elements in the list are alternatives, so the rule allows the union. Multiple policies that select the same pod are also additive: the allowed set is the union of every policy's allows, and there is no way to write an explicit deny rule in the NetworkPolicy API.
details: To allow a namespace's pods plus a specific pod elsewhere, use two separate peer elements rather than one combined element.
An empty `from: []` or a rule with no peers allows all sources for that direction and port combination.
Cluster-scoped admin network policies are a separate API (AdminNetworkPolicy, alpha in recent releases) and are not part of networking.k8s.io/v1 NetworkPolicy.
pitfalls: Combining namespaceSelector and podSelector in one element and expecting either to match.
Expecting a second policy to restrict what the first allows; policies only add permissions.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-allow-web
  namespace: team-alpha
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: frontend
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8443
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 53
configs.purpose: Allow only web pods in the frontend namespace to reach api on 8443, and allow DNS egress to kube-system.

mcqs.question: A policy rule has one peer with namespaceSelector team-alpha and podSelector app=web. Which traffic matches?
options: Any pod in team-alpha or any pod labeled app=web anywhere
Only pods in team-alpha that also have app=web
All pods in the cluster
No traffic, because two selectors cannot be combined
mcqs.rationale: Selectors within the same peer element are ANDed. OR semantics require separate elements in the from or to list.

misconceptions.claim: Writing a NetworkPolicy with an empty podSelector and no rules creates a deny-all that overrides other policies.
misconceptions.correction: Policies are additive. A policy with no rules denies nothing by itself unless it isolates a direction for the selected pods, and even then other policies can add allows. There is no deny rule in the core NetworkPolicy API.

references.title: Kubernetes Documentation: Network Policies (behavior of selectors)

facts.title: Pod Security Admission enforces privileged, baseline or restricted per namespace
facts.fact: Pod Security Admission, stable since Kubernetes 1.25, replaces PodSecurityPolicy and applies one of three levels to a namespace through labels. Privileged is unrestricted, baseline blocks known privilege escalations, and restricted adds strong controls such as non-root execution, dropped capabilities and a seccomp profile. The labels can enforce, warn or audit independently, and the version label pins the policy semantics so a cluster upgrade does not silently change what is allowed.
details: Restricted requires `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`, `runAsNonRoot: true`, `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` and disallows hostPath, hostPort, hostNetwork and privileged containers.
`pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.29` pins the checks to the 1.29 policy; `latest` follows the cluster version.
Exemptions for namespaces and users are configured on the admission controller, not in namespace labels, and should be minimal.
pitfalls: Applying restricted to an existing namespace without a dry run, causing production pods to be rejected on their next rollout.
Using warn or audit only and assuming workloads are actually being blocked.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-alpha
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.29
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
configs.purpose: Enforce the Kubernetes 1.29 restricted profile in a namespace, with warnings and audit records for violations.

commands.purpose: Ask the API server to evaluate the label change without persisting it, surfacing existing violations.

mcqs.question: Which control is required by the restricted Pod Security Standard but not by baseline?
options: No privileged containers
No hostPath volumes
runAsNonRoot with allowPrivilegeEscalation false and capabilities dropped to ALL
No hostNetwork
mcqs.rationale: Baseline already blocks privileged containers, hostPath, hostNetwork and hostPort. Restricted adds the non-root, no-escalation, capability and seccomp requirements.

facts.title: Gatekeeper and Kyverno both sit on validating admission webhooks, with different authoring models
facts.fact: OPA Gatekeeper deploys a validating webhook and evaluates ConstraintTemplates written in Rego, instantiated as Constraints that select resources and set an enforcement action. Kyverno evaluates YAML-native ClusterPolicies that can validate, mutate, generate or verify image signatures. Both fail closed or open according to the webhook's failurePolicy, so an unavailable policy engine with `failurePolicy: Fail` can block all matching admissions, including repairs.
details: Gatekeeper's `enforcementAction` supports deny, warn and dryrun; the audit controller reports existing violations separately.
Kyverno `validationFailureAction: Enforce` blocks, while `Audit` only reports; policy reports are produced as custom resources.
Both engines need exemptions or namespace exclusions for kube-system so a bad policy cannot take down the control plane.
pitfalls: Setting failurePolicy Fail on a webhook that matches every resource without excluding the policy engine's own namespace.
Assuming a policy engine replaces Pod Security Admission; PSA is built in and cannot be uninstalled by a misconfigured webhook.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8srequiredlabels
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sRequiredLabels
      validation:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            labels:
              type: array
              items:
                type: string
  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
      rego: |
        package k8srequiredlabels

        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          required := input.parameters.labels[_]
          not input.review.object.metadata.labels[required]
          msg := sprintf("missing required label %v", [required])
        }
configs.purpose: Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate that flags objects missing labels listed in the constraint parameters.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-nonroot
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  background: true
  rules:
    - name: check-run-as-nonroot
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
      validate:
        message: "runAsNonRoot must be true and privilege escalation disabled"
        pattern:
          spec:
            securityContext:
              runAsNonRoot: true
            containers:
              - securityContext:
                  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
configs.purpose: Kyverno ClusterPolicy that rejects pods which do not declare the required security context.

mcqs.question: What is the main availability risk of a cluster-wide validating admission webhook with failurePolicy: Fail?
options: It silently allows all traffic when the engine is down
If the webhook is unavailable, matching API writes fail, potentially blocking workloads and repairs
It disables RBAC
It prevents image pulls
mcqs.rationale: Fail-closed webhooks reject requests when the backend cannot be reached. The blast radius must be limited with scoped matches, namespace exclusions and a highly available policy deployment.

facts.title: EncryptionConfiguration protects Secrets in etcd, and provider order matters
facts.fact: The API server encrypts designated resources at rest when started with an EncryptionConfiguration, typically Secrets and sometimes ConfigMaps. Providers are tried in order for writes and any provider in the list can decrypt an existing value; placing `identity` first means new writes are stored in plaintext. A KMS provider keeps the data encryption key wrapped by an external key service, while `aescbc` stores the key in the configuration file and therefore only moves the problem to file protection.
details: After enabling encryption, existing Secrets remain readable but are not re-encrypted until they are written again; rewriting them completes the migration.
The configuration file contains key material with `aescbc` and must be readable only by the API server process.
Encryption at rest does not restrict API access; RBAC on Secrets and audit logging remain necessary.
pitfalls: Leaving `identity` as the first provider after a migration, which silently writes new Secrets unencrypted.
Backing up etcd without protecting the encryption keys, or storing the keys beside the backup.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]
    providers:
      - kms:
          apiVersion: v2
          name: app-kms
          endpoint: unix:///var/run/kmsplugin/socket.sock
          timeout: 3s
      - identity: {}
configs.purpose: Encrypt Secrets and ConfigMaps through a KMS v2 provider, with identity only as a read fallback.

commands.code: kubectl get secrets -n team-alpha -o json | kubectl replace -f -
commands.purpose: Rewrite Secrets so they are stored using the current first encryption provider.

mcqs.question: An EncryptionConfiguration lists identity before the kms provider. What is the effect on newly written Secrets?
options: They are encrypted with KMS because KMS is more secure
They are stored in plaintext because the first provider is used for writes
They are encrypted with both providers
The API server refuses to start
mcqs.rationale: The first provider performs writes; later providers are only used to decrypt existing data. Identity first means plaintext storage, so order the real provider first.

misconceptions.claim: Enabling encryption at rest means an attacker with cluster read access can no longer read Secrets.
misconceptions.correction: Encryption at rest protects the etcd data files and backups. Anyone authorized to call the API server for Secrets still receives decrypted values, so RBAC and audit logging remain the primary access controls.

references.title: Kubernetes Documentation: Encrypting Confidential Data at Rest

facts.title: External secret stores remove secrets from Git, not from the cluster
facts.fact: The External Secrets Operator reconciles an ExternalSecret custom resource into a native Kubernetes Secret by fetching values from a store such as AWS Secrets Manager, Vault or GCP Secret Manager. This removes secret material from Git and centralizes rotation, but the synced Secret still exists in etcd and is still readable by anyone with `get secrets` in the namespace. Authentication from the operator to the cloud provider should use workload identity federation rather than a static key.
details: `refreshInterval` controls how often the operator re-reads the upstream value; rotation is only as fast as that interval plus pod restart or reload.
A ClusterSecretStore is cluster-scoped and needs careful RBAC so one tenant cannot reference another tenant's store.
`dataFrom` can pull an entire upstream secret into the Kubernetes Secret, which broadens exposure compared with explicit `data` keys.
pitfalls: Granting the operator a wildcard read on every secret in the cloud account.
Believing that using External Secrets makes etcd encryption unnecessary.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
  namespace: team-alpha
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secrets-manager
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: db-credentials
  data:
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/team-alpha/db
        property: password
configs.purpose: Sync one password from an external store into a namespaced Kubernetes Secret.

mcqs.question: After adopting External Secrets, what still needs to be true for the synced credential to be protected at rest?
options: Nothing, the external store encrypts it end to end
The Kubernetes Secret still needs etcd encryption and restricted RBAC
The Secret must be stored in a ConfigMap
The operator must run as root
mcqs.rationale: The operator materializes a normal Secret in the cluster. That object persists in etcd and is governed by Kubernetes authorization, so encryption at rest and RBAC still apply.

references.title: Kubernetes Documentation: Good practices for Kubernetes Secrets

facts.title: The API server is the cluster's front door and should not be on the public internet by default
facts.fact: Every Kubernetes API request is authenticated and authorized by the API server, so its network exposure and authentication settings define the cluster's real perimeter. Anonymous authentication should be disabled, authorization should include Node and RBAC, and audit logging should be enabled. Managed clusters often expose a public endpoint by default; restricting it to known CIDRs or switching to private access removes a large brute-force and credential-stuffing surface.
details: `--anonymous-auth=false` removes unauthenticated requests; `--authorization-mode=Node,RBAC` keeps the node authorizer plus RBAC.
`--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction` limits what a kubelet identity can modify.
The API server's serving certificate should be signed by a CA the kubelet trusts, and `--kubelet-certificate-authority` enables verification of the kubelet serving certificate.
pitfalls: Leaving the endpoint public with a permissive CIDR such as 0.0.0.0/0 and relying on authentication alone.
Disabling the Node authorizer while keeping kubelets able to read Secrets cluster-wide.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: kube-apiserver
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  containers:
    - name: kube-apiserver
      image: registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.29.4
      command:
        - kube-apiserver
        - --anonymous-auth=false
        - --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
        - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction
        - --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit/policy.yaml
        - --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
        - --kubelet-certificate-authority=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
configs.purpose: Illustrative static pod manifest with anonymous auth disabled, Node plus RBAC authorization and audit logging.

commands.purpose: Disable the public EKS API endpoint and rely on private access.

mcqs.question: Which combination most directly reduces the API server's unauthenticated attack surface?
options: anonymous-auth=false plus a private or CIDR-restricted endpoint
Enabling the AlwaysPullImages admission plugin
Setting a longer service account token lifetime
Disabling audit logging to reduce load
mcqs.rationale: Disabling anonymous authentication removes unauthenticated identity, and restricting endpoint reachability removes internet-wide exposure. The other options either do not affect authentication or weaken detection.

facts.title: The kubelet API can run commands and must use webhook authn and authz
facts.fact: The kubelet exposes an HTTPS API on port 10250 that supports exec, logs and pod status, and an unauthenticated read-only endpoint on 10255 in older configurations. Hardening requires disabling anonymous authentication, enabling webhook authentication and authorization so the API server's TokenReview and SubjectAccessReview decide access, and setting `readOnlyPort` to 0. Without this, anyone who can reach the node's kubelet port may be able to execute commands in pods or read their logs.
details: `authentication.webhook.enabled: true` plus `authorization.mode: Webhook` delegates decisions to the API server.
`authentication.x509.clientCAFile` lets the kubelet validate client certificates from the cluster CA.
NodeRestriction and the Node authorizer limit a compromised node's ability to read unrelated Secrets.
pitfalls: Assuming network policy protects the kubelet port; the kubelet is on the node network, outside pod NetworkPolicy scope.
Leaving anonymous auth enabled because `kubectl logs` worked without noticing why.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: false
  webhook:
    enabled: true
  x509:
    clientCAFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
authorization:
  mode: Webhook
readOnlyPort: 0
configs.purpose: Kubelet configuration that disables anonymous access and delegates authorization to the API server.

commands.purpose: Check whether the kubelet ports answer without credentials on a documentation address.

mcqs.question: What does kubelet authorization mode Webhook do?
options: Uses a local policy file on each node
Sends SubjectAccessReview requests to the API server to decide access
Allows all requests from the node's pod CIDR
Disables the kubelet API entirely
mcqs.rationale: Webhook mode delegates authorization decisions to the API server, so cluster RBAC governs kubelet API access. It does not disable the API or rely on a local file.

facts.title: Audit rules are first-match, and RequestResponse captures object bodies
facts.fact: The API server audit policy is an ordered list of rules; the first rule that matches an event sets its level, and later rules are ignored. Levels are None, Metadata, Request, RequestResponse, with increasing detail and cost. RequestResponse records request and response bodies, which can include Secret data, so it should be scoped to namespaces or resources that need it rather than applied cluster-wide.
details: `omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]` avoids duplicate entries for long-running requests.
Audit backends include log files and webhooks; a webhook backend must be highly available or the API server can block.
A common pattern is Metadata for most resources, Request for Secrets so bodies are excluded, and RequestResponse for a specific investigation namespace.
pitfalls: Putting a broad catch-all rule first, which makes every later rule unreachable.
Enabling RequestResponse for Secrets cluster-wide and shipping the audit log to a lower-trust system.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]
rules:
  - level: None
    users: ["system:kube-proxy"]
    verbs: ["watch"]
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["endpoints", "services"]
  - level: Metadata
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]
  - level: RequestResponse
    namespaces: ["team-alpha"]
  - level: Metadata
configs.purpose: Audit policy that skips proxy watches, records only metadata for Secrets, and captures full bodies in one namespace.

mcqs.question: Why is a cluster-wide RequestResponse audit rule risky for Secrets?
options: It disables RBAC
The audit log records request and response bodies, which can contain Secret data
It prevents the API server from starting
It causes Secrets to be stored unencrypted in etcd
mcqs.rationale: RequestResponse includes object bodies. For Secrets that means credential material in the audit backend, which must then be protected and retained like a secret store.

misconceptions.claim: Audit rules are evaluated in order and the most specific rule wins regardless of position.
misconceptions.correction: Evaluation stops at the first matching rule. Specific rules must be placed before broad catch-alls, otherwise they never take effect.

facts.title: A namespace is an API scope, not a security boundary between hostile tenants
facts.fact: Namespaces partition names and provide a natural place for RBAC, quotas and network policy, but they do not isolate nodes, the kernel, the container runtime or cluster-scoped resources. A tenant that can create pods can often reach the kubelet, mount host paths if admission allows it, or consume shared resources. Hostile multi-tenancy therefore needs defence in depth: per-tenant RBAC and quotas, default-deny network policy, Pod Security Admission, node pools or separate clusters, and sandboxed runtimes for untrusted code.
details: Cluster-scoped resources such as CustomResourceDefinitions, PersistentVolumes and Nodes are shared and require explicit access control.
ResourceQuota limits aggregate consumption but does not stop a tenant from exhausting node-level resources such as process IDs.
Sandboxed runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers add a user-space or VM boundary when the kernel is shared.
pitfalls: Treating separate namespaces as sufficient isolation for customers who run arbitrary code.
Granting a tenant the ability to create PersistentVolumeClaims without storage class restrictions or quotas.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: tenant-quota
  namespace: team-alpha
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "8"
    requests.memory: 16Gi
    limits.cpu: "16"
    limits.memory: 32Gi
    persistentvolumeclaims: "4"
    count/pods: "40"
configs.purpose: Cap a tenant namespace's aggregate resource consumption and object count.

configs.snippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: tenant-defaults
  namespace: team-alpha
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 512Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 2Gi
configs.purpose: Provide default and maximum container resources so unset pods cannot request unbounded capacity.

mcqs.question: Two hostile customers run arbitrary code in separate namespaces of one cluster. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Namespaces provide VM-level isolation, so this is safe
Namespaces alone are insufficient; node isolation, admission control and sandboxed runtimes are needed
NetworkPolicy alone makes the tenants safe
ResourceQuota prevents container escapes
mcqs.rationale: Namespaces scope API objects, not kernel or node resources. Hostile tenants need stronger boundaries such as separate node pools or clusters and sandboxed runtimes, plus RBAC, policy and quotas.

misconceptions.claim: Because Kubernetes namespaces are a security boundary, a tenant cannot affect another tenant's workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Namespaces are an API and policy scope. Tenants share the control plane, nodes and kernel unless you add node isolation, sandboxing and strict admission control, so a kernel or runtime escape crosses tenant boundaries.

references.title: NIST SP 800-190: Application Container Security Guide

facts.title: Base64 in a Secret manifest is encoding, not protection
facts.fact: The `data` field of a Kubernetes Secret holds base64-encoded bytes, and `stringData` accepts plain strings that the API server encodes on write. Base64 is reversible by anyone, so a Secret committed to Git or readable through RBAC is exposed. Protection comes from keeping Secret manifests out of source control, restricting `get`, `list` and `watch` on Secrets, enabling encryption at rest, and rotating credentials when exposure is suspected.
details: `kubectl get secret db-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d` recovers the value, which is exactly what an attacker with read access does.
RBAC cannot hide a Secret's contents from a subject allowed to read the object; it can only deny the whole object.
Sealed Secrets and SOPS encrypt the manifest at rest in Git, but the decrypted Secret still exists in the cluster.
pitfalls: Committing a Secret manifest and assuming the base64 text is obfuscated enough.
Granting list or watch on all Secrets for convenience, which exposes every credential in the namespace.

commands.code: kubectl get secret db-credentials -n team-alpha -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d; echo
commands.purpose: Decode a Secret value to demonstrate that base64 is not encryption.

commands.code: kubectl auth can-i list secrets -n team-alpha --as=system:serviceaccount:team-alpha:report-reader
commands.purpose: Check whether a service account can enumerate Secrets in the namespace.

mcqs.question: A Secret manifest is committed to a public repository with base64 data. What is the correct conclusion?
options: The value is safe because it is base64-encoded
The value is exposed and should be treated as compromised and rotated
Only cluster administrators can decode it
The value is protected by etcd encryption
mcqs.rationale: Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode it, and etcd encryption does not apply to a copy in Git, so the credential must be rotated.

misconceptions.claim: Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted, which is why they are not stored as plain YAML.
misconceptions.correction: By default a Secret is stored as base64-encoded data in etcd. Encryption at rest is a separate opt-in configuration, and neither encoding nor encryption removes the need to control RBAC access.

references.title: Kubernetes Documentation: Good practices for Kubernetes Secrets

facts.title: Private package names must resolve to the private registry first
facts.fact: Dependency confusion exploits a resolver that prefers a public registry for a package name an organization also uses internally. An attacker publishes a package with the same name and a higher version to the public registry, and a build that checks both sources installs the attacker's package. Mitigations map each internal scope or index explicitly, make the private registry authoritative for internal names, reserve internal names publicly, and verify the resolved URL in the lockfile.
details: npm scopes (`@acme/...`) can be bound to a registry in `.npmrc`, so the scope never falls through to the public registry.
pip's `--extra-index-url` does not express priority; pip considers candidates from every configured index and selects the best version, which is exactly the attack condition.
A package's `resolved` field in a lockfile should point at the internal registry for internal dependencies.
pitfalls: Using `--extra-index-url` for the private index while leaving PyPI as the default index.
Assuming an internal package is safe because it is not published publicly; the attacker only needs the name.

configs.purpose: npm configuration that sends every @acme package to the internal registry while other packages use the public one.

commands.code:
npm config get registry
npm view @acme/billing-sdk version --registry=https://npm.example.internal/repository/npm-private/
commands.purpose: Confirm the effective registry and that the internal package resolves internally.
Check that internal packages resolve to the internal registry in the lockfile.

mcqs.question: Why does adding a private index with pip's --extra-index-url fail to prevent dependency confusion?
options: pip ignores extra indexes when a private index is present
pip compares versions across all indexes and can select a higher public version
pip cannot install from HTTPS
extra indexes are only used for wheels
mcqs.rationale: pip does not treat one index as authoritative. It gathers candidates from all indexes and picks the best version, so a higher public version of an internal name wins unless version pinning or hashes prevent it.

misconceptions.claim: Publishing internal packages under a unique name is enough protection against dependency confusion.
misconceptions.correction: Uniqueness is not secrecy: an attacker can still publish the same name if it is unclaimed publicly. You need registry scoping, an authoritative index, name reservation and resolution checks.

facts.title: Lookalike package names trade on a developer's typo
facts.fact: Typosquatting registers names that are one edit away from popular packages, or that use visually similar characters, and waits for a mistyped install. The malicious package may run an install script, exfiltrate environment variables or pull a second-stage payload. Defences include exact-name allowlists for production dependencies, disabling install scripts where possible, checking repository and maintainer metadata for new dependencies, and requiring review for any new package.
details: npm `postinstall` scripts run automatically; `npm ci --ignore-scripts` avoids them at the cost of packages that legitimately need a build step.
Provenance attestations link a published package to a source repository and build, making an unattributed copy easier to spot.
Internal mirrors that proxy a public registry still need name review; a proxy does not judge intent.
pitfalls: Letting an automated tool add the first search result for a package name without checking the repository URL.
Assuming a package with many downloads is trustworthy; typosquats can inherit download noise or be installed by bots.

mcqs.question: Which control most directly reduces the risk of a mistyped package name entering production?
options: Running the container as non-root
Requiring an explicit reviewed allowlist of dependency names and versions
Enabling read-only root filesystems
Rotating registry credentials
mcqs.rationale: An allowlist prevents an unapproved name from being installed at all, which addresses the typo before code runs. The other controls reduce impact but do not stop the wrong package from being fetched.

facts.title: Lockfiles and hash pinning make installs deterministic, not automatically safe
facts.fact: A lockfile records the exact resolved version and, for npm, an integrity hash and resolved URL for each package; `npm ci` installs strictly from it instead of re-resolving ranges. For Python, `pip install --require-hashes` refuses any requirement without a matching hash, which also forces every transitive dependency to be pinned. These controls prevent silent version drift and registry substitution, but they do not help if the compromised version was already recorded in the lockfile.
details: Lockfile changes should be reviewed like code changes, especially new `resolved` hosts and unexpected transitive additions.
Hash pinning requires pinning transitive dependencies too, which is why constraints files and lock generators are commonly used.
A lockfile is only as trustworthy as the review of the diff that introduced it.
pitfalls: Running `npm install` in CI, which can rewrite the lockfile and resolve versions the review never saw.
Adding hashes for direct dependencies only and leaving transitive packages unhashed.

configs.purpose: Excerpt showing the version, resolved URL and integrity hash that a lockfile records per package.

mcqs.question: What does `npm ci` do differently from `npm install`?
options: It ignores the lockfile and resolves the newest versions
It installs exactly what the lockfile specifies and fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree
It runs install scripts twice
It only installs production dependencies
mcqs.rationale: npm ci is intended for automation: it removes node_modules, installs from the lockfile without rewriting it, and errors when the manifest and lockfile are inconsistent.

facts.title: A reproducible build lets an independent party confirm the artifact matches the source
facts.fact: A build is reproducible when rebuilding the same source with the same inputs yields bit-identical output. That property lets a third party rebuild from source and compare hashes, which detects a compromised build service or a tampered artifact. Achieving it requires removing nondeterminism such as timestamps, absolute paths, randomized map ordering and unstable archive metadata, and pinning the toolchain and dependency versions.
details: `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` is the standard convention for clamping embedded timestamps.
Go builds benefit from `-trimpath` and a fixed build ID; many ecosystems need normalization of file modes and ordering in archives.
Reproducibility is a property to measure, not a claim: publish the rebuild instructions and compare hashes for each release.
pitfalls: Assuming a hermetic CI system automatically produces reproducible artifacts; embedded timestamps and paths still vary.
Comparing container image tags instead of digests, which hides differences behind a mutable reference.

commands.purpose: Build with a fixed epoch and record the artifact hash for a second independent build.
Explain remaining byte differences between two builds.

mcqs.question: Two builds of the same commit produce artifacts with different hashes. Which cause is most consistent with a reproducibility problem rather than a source change?
options: An embedded build timestamp and absolute build path
A different commit SHA in the source
A different dependency version in the lockfile
A changed compiler major version
mcqs.rationale: Timestamps and paths vary between otherwise identical builds. The other options change the inputs, so different output would be expected and is not a reproducibility defect.

facts.title: SLSA v1.0 separates build levels from source levels
facts.fact: SLSA v1.0 defines Build levels 1 through 3 and Source levels 1 through 4, rather than a single ladder. Build L1 means provenance exists and describes the build; L2 requires signed provenance generated by a hosted build service; L3 requires a hardened build platform with strong isolation and non-falsifiable provenance. Source levels address source review, history integrity and provenance of the source itself, so an artifact can be Build L3 while the source controls remain weak.
details: Provenance is an in-toto attestation with a subject digest and a predicate describing the build.
Earlier SLSA v0.1 used four build levels; v1.0 reduced the build track to three and added a separate source track.
SLSA levels describe the integrity of the build process, not the absence of vulnerabilities in the code.
pitfalls: Claiming SLSA L3 from a CI job that signs its own provenance on a shared, mutable runner.
Treating a level as a compliance badge without checking which track and which threats it covers.

configs.purpose: Minimal SLSA v1 provenance attestation binding an image digest to a builder and source URI.

mcqs.question: In SLSA v1.0, what distinguishes Build level 3 from Build level 2?
options: L3 requires source code review; L2 does not
L3 requires a hardened, isolated build platform and non-falsifiable provenance
L3 requires a signed commit for every change
L3 requires reproducible builds by definition
mcqs.rationale: L2 requires signed provenance from a hosted build service. L3 adds a hardened build environment whose provenance cannot be forged by the build itself. Source review is on the separate Source track, and reproducibility is not a level requirement.

misconceptions.claim: SLSA level 3 proves the software contains no known vulnerabilities.
misconceptions.correction: SLSA measures build integrity and provenance. It says nothing about the security of the code or its dependencies; vulnerability management and review are separate controls.

facts.title: Verification must pin the expected builder and source, not just check a signature
facts.fact: Verifying provenance means checking that the attestation is signed by a trusted builder, that its subject digest matches the artifact being deployed, and that its source URI and build parameters match expectations. A signature check alone proves only that some key signed some statement. Deployment gates should encode the trusted builder identity and the allowed source repository, and reject artifacts whose provenance is missing or describes a different digest.
details: `slsa-verifier verify-image` checks the subject digest, source URI and builder identity against expected values.
`cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance` verifies the attestation signature and certificate identity.
Pinning a builder identity is what prevents an attacker who controls a different CI project from producing a validly signed but untrusted artifact.
pitfalls: Accepting any attestation whose signature validates, including one from a forked repository's workflow.
Verifying provenance at build time only, while the deployment path pulls by tag with no verification.

commands.purpose: Verify that the image digest was built from the expected repository and tag.
Verify the provenance attestation signature and the exact workflow identity that produced it.

mcqs.question: An admission policy accepts any validly signed SLSA provenance. What is the main gap?
options: It does not check the artifact digest
It does not constrain the builder or source, so untrusted producers can satisfy it
It requires too much CPU
It verifies the SBOM instead of the image
mcqs.rationale: A valid signature only proves control of a signing identity. Without pinning the expected builder and source, any producer with a trusted issuer can create acceptable provenance.

facts.title: Pin third-party CI actions to a commit SHA, not a tag
facts.fact: A GitHub Actions reference such as `owner/action@v3` is a mutable tag, and the tag owner or a compromised account can repoint it to different code. Referencing a full 40-character commit SHA binds the workflow to exact content, and Dependabot or Renovate can still propose updates. Pinning should be combined with least-privilege workflow permissions, because a pinned action still runs with whatever token and secrets the job exposes.
details: The `uses` value is the primary supply-chain control for actions; `@main` and major-version tags are both mutable.
Review the diff when a bot bumps a pinned SHA; the pin moves trust from a tag to a reviewed commit.
Container actions and reusable workflows have the same pinning concern, and reusable workflows should also be referenced by commit.
pitfalls: Pinning actions but leaving `permissions: write-all` on the workflow.
Using `pull_request_target` and checking out the fork's head, which runs untrusted code with a privileged token and secrets.

configs.snippet:
name: test
on: [pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683
      - run: make test
configs.purpose: Workflow pinned to a full checkout commit SHA with read-only token permissions.

mcqs.question: Why is `uses: example/action@v2` weaker than `uses: example/action@<full-commit-sha>`?
options: Tags cannot be resolved by GitHub Actions
The tag is mutable and can be repointed to different code
The SHA reference disables caching
Tags do not support inputs
mcqs.rationale: Version tags are movable references. A commit SHA identifies exact content, so a changed tag or compromised maintainer cannot silently alter what the workflow runs.

facts.title: Each CI job should hold only the permissions that job needs
facts.fact: CI workflows commonly inherit a broad default token and access to every repository secret. Least privilege means declaring permissions explicitly, ideally denying by default at the workflow level and granting per job, separating build from deploy, and scoping cloud access with OIDC and environment protections. Secrets available to a job are available to every step in it, including third-party actions and any code the job checks out and executes.
details: GitHub Actions supports `permissions: {}` at workflow level and a narrower `permissions` block per job.
Environment protection rules can require approval and restrict which branches may deploy.
Build jobs should not hold production credentials; the deploy job should assume a separate role after an approval gate.
pitfalls: Assuming secret masking prevents exfiltration; masking only redacts log output.
Reusing one long-lived deploy credential for every environment and every branch.

permissions: {}

  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:

mcqs.question: A pull-request workflow needs to compile code but not publish anything. Which permission set is closest to least privilege?
options: contents: write, packages: write, id-token: write
contents: read only
No permissions block, using the repository default
actions: write and deployments: write
mcqs.rationale: Compiling needs to read the repository. Write scopes, OIDC tokens and deployment permissions should be absent unless the job actually publishes or deploys.

facts.title: Shared build caches are a trust boundary that untrusted jobs must not write to
facts.fact: Compiler caches, remote Bazel caches, container layer caches and CI dependency caches can return artifacts produced by a different job. If an untrusted pull request or branch can write to a cache that a trusted build later restores, it can substitute a compiled object, a package or a layer without touching source. Cache keys derived from untrusted input make targeted poisoning easier. The safe design separates caches by trust domain, makes caches read-only for untrusted jobs, and verifies artifact digests after restore.
details: GitHub Actions caches are scoped so a pull request cannot overwrite the base branch cache, but self-hosted and externally shared caches often lack that scoping.
Cache keys should include a hash of the trusted inputs and a trust-domain identifier, not a branch name supplied by the contributor.
A cache hit is an optimization, not an integrity check; verify hashes or signatures before using restored outputs.
pitfalls: Letting fork pull requests populate a cache consumed by release builds.
Assuming a cache is safe because the key includes a commit SHA, when the attacker can choose the commit and the key.
Restoring a container layer cache across projects that do not share a trust level.

configs.snippet:
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.cache/go-build
    key: go-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/go.sum') }}
    restore-keys: |
      go-${{ runner.os }}-
configs.purpose: Illustrative cache step; in a shared-runner design the same cache must not be writable by untrusted jobs.

mcqs.question: Why is a shared remote build cache dangerous when untrusted pull requests can write to it?
options: It increases storage cost
A later trusted build may restore attacker-produced objects instead of compiling from reviewed source
It disables compiler warnings
It prevents reproducible builds
mcqs.rationale: A cache lookup can return content the trusted build did not produce. Without separation or verification, that content is incorporated into the release artifact.

misconceptions.claim: Including the commit SHA in a cache key makes cache poisoning impossible.
misconceptions.correction: An attacker who controls a branch or pull request also controls the commit, and can shape the key. Isolation by trust domain and read-only caches for untrusted jobs are the controls, not key uniqueness.

facts.title: A signed commit proves key possession, not review or safety
facts.fact: Git commit signing with GPG or SSH keys produces a signature over the commit object, and `git verify-commit` checks it against a trusted key. Platforms can display a verified badge and enforce that protected branches require signed commits. Signing binds a commit to whoever held the key at signing time; it does not prove the code was reviewed, that the author understood it, or that the key was not stolen.
details: SSH signing requires Git 2.34 or later and an `ssh` signing format configured with `gpg.format`.
Signed tags are more relevant for releases than individual commits; verify the tag before building from it.
Key revocation and rotation are part of the control: a compromised signing key must be revoked and its signatures re-examined.
pitfalls: Treating a verified badge as evidence of code review.
Requiring signed commits on a branch without protecting the branch from force pushes or direct writes.

mcqs.question: What does a valid commit signature prove?
options: The code was reviewed by a maintainer
The commit content matches what the holder of the signing key signed
The commit contains no vulnerabilities
The commit was built reproducibly
mcqs.rationale: A signature binds the commit object to a key. Review, vulnerability status and build reproducibility are separate properties not established by signing.

misconceptions.claim: Enforcing signed commits on the main branch secures the supply chain end to end.
misconceptions.correction: Signed commits only attest authorship of commit objects. You still need protected branches, review, signed tags or artifacts, build provenance and deployment verification to cover the rest of the chain.
